guideText.text: North Channel is a left-favouring reef break sitting outside the shallow reef north of Mombasa, and it's sometimes called Leven Reef. It's a much shorter paddle than the South Channel, and less sharky too. The waves break over dead coral, and the wider setting is worth knowing about: miles of white powdery sand with a reef 2km offshore create a natural lagoon that's ideal for kitesurfing with Prosurf Kite.

La Passe

Overview

La Passe is a right-hand reef break that peels over dead coral, tucked into a gap in the reef a little further north, before Anse Royale. It suits intermediate surfers and is more of a rare treat than a reliable session. When It Works

La Passe is inconsistent, but it can turn on beautifully when the setup lines up. It draws swell from southeast through south, with south swell the best match. The wave works from 0.9 m / 3 ft to 3 m / 10 ft, so there is scope from smaller days through to solid overhead surf, and its better sessions tend to come on a southeast swell. Wind and Tide

Look for northwest offshore wind to groom it. It breaks across low, mid, and high tide, but a rising tide is generally the better call. Local Tips

This is an intermediate-level wave over shallow coral, best for surfers confident in that setting. Expect a moderately busy lineup when it is working.

guideText.text: Police Bay in Mahe is an exposed reef break that has fairly consistent surf. Winter is the best time of year for surfing here. The best wind direction is from the north. Waves just as likely from local windswells as from distant groundswells and the ideal swell angle is from the southeast. Reef breaks provide lefts and rights. Rarely crowded here. Police Bay is one of the most exposed beaches on the island, sitting next to Anse Petite Police and running the longer of the two. It's a beach break with both lefts and rights peeling over a patchy mix of uneven reef and sand. Be realistic about it, though: it's usually a rocky shore dump with strong currents, so it's rarely worth a dedicated trip.

guideText.text: Le Port in West Reunion is an exposed reef break that does not work very often. Winter is the best time of year for surfing here. The best wind direction is from the east. Most of the surf here comes from groundswells and the best swell direction is from the southwest. A reef breaks right. Rarely crowded here. Beware of sharks and rocks. Le Port

Le Port is a big-wave reef peak sitting just north of the Possession Harbour entrance. It breaks both left and right over an uneven reef, and it stays rarely ridden and hard to find. When It Works The peak draws swell from southwest through southeast, with southwest (SW) swell the best match. It works from 1.2 m / 4 ft to 3.7 m / 12 ft , so it needs real size before it starts to break. Consistency is on the patchy side, so expect to wait for the right window rather than count on it. Wind and Tide Look for east (E) offshore wind to clean it up. The reef can work through low, mid, and high tide, with a rising tide generally the better call. Local Tips This one suits intermediate surfers, and the lineup usually stays fairly quiet. Keep in mind it carries a serious shark factor, so know what you are paddling into before you go.

guideText.text: Saint Leu in West Reunion is an exposed point break that has dependable surf. Winter is the best time of year for surfing here. Offshore winds blow from the southeast. Tends to receive a mix of groundswells and windswells and the ideal swell direction is from the west southwest.The waves is a point break that peels left. A fairly popluar wave that can sometimes get crowded Take care of urchins, sharks,fire coral. Saint Leu

Saint-Leu is a world-class left-hand reef break and one of the best waves in the area when it turns on. The famous lefts start with a quick drop into an open-face wall made for carving big turns, then bend sharply around the reef into a couple of bowly, hollow sections that throw out a shallow tube. When it is overhead the sections link up for a ride of around 300 metres; on smaller days it still works, just in shorter sections. When It Works The reef draws swell from south to southwest and comes alive when stronger southwest swells push through, usually in winter, so southwest (SW) is the direction to look for. It works from 0.6 m / 2 ft to 3 m / 10 ft , though it really needs to be overhead before the full wave links end to end. Consistency is moderate, so plan around the swell windows rather than expecting it every session. Wind and Tide Look for southeast (SE) offshore wind to clean up the wall.
